articles.title: 5 2000s Superhero Movies I Wish I Could See All Over Again, Like the Best X-Men Sequel Ever
articles.summary: If you're looking for the best decade for superhero movies, the 2010s feel like the peak. articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google If you're looking for the best decade for superhero movies , the 2010s feel like the peak. The MCU was firing on all cylinders, animated superhero projects were better than ever, DC delivered some legitimate classics, and some of the deeper-cut comics like Kick-Ass and Kingsman were brought to life. However, the 2000s were the most important era for the genre. In the decades prior, we really only had memorable films surrounding Batman and Superman, and even those characters received lackluster sequels. It was difficult to take superhero movies seriously, but that began to change in a major way when the 2000s rolled around.

Following the underrated success of Blade in 1998, the 2000s started with even bigger hits in X-Men and Spider-Man . That started a slew of superhero movies that included some totally original and outstanding ideas, reboots for both Batman and Superman, and the beginning of long-running franchises that changed the face of the superhero genre. I have now seen these classics over and over in the years since their release, but it would be incredible to experience them for the first time again. That includes the best X-Men sequel, which is even more crucial to remember heading into Avengers: Doomsday .

The entire Marvel Cinematic Universe doesn't happen if Iron Man doesn't succeed in 2008. The film was a risk at the time, centering on someone who wasn't an "A-list" Marvel hero and led by an actor who was controversial. However, Robert Downey Jr. delivered a rockstar performance that turned his career around and launched the highest-grossing film franchise in Hollywood history. The first time watching Iron Man was interesting because for most of the runtime, it felt like a good, but standard superhero flick.

You're completely captivated by Downey Jr., though, and it's hard to match what it felt like to watch an iconic star and character rise to prominence. The experience gets taken to the next level right at the end when Tony Stark reveals his true identity to the masses. That wasn't something I was used to in superhero movies and helped Iron Man stand out. Seeing the birth of the MCU for the first time again would be beautiful.

The greatest sequel in the history of X-Men movies was the very first, which is 2003's X2: X-Men United . The first installment in the franchise remains a fun ride but getting to see this follow-up take everything that worked there and turn it up a notch was incredible. It starts right from the opening scene, where Nightcrawler gets introduced as he uses his stunning mutant ability to infiltrate the White House. As soon as that scene was over, you knew you were witnessing something special.

X2 also featured the Brotherhood of Mutants tentatively teaming up with the X-Men to turn back the threat of William Stryker's plan, which was a sight to behold. From the always masterful interplay between Professor X and Magneto to Wolverine fighting Deathstrike to Jean Grey's emotional sacrifice, nearly everything about X2 worked. It's easy to be jealous of the people who are seeing it for the first time before the characters return in Avengers: Doomsday .

After the success of films like Spider-Man and X-Men , Brad Bird and Pixar released their very own completely original superhero movie. That was a bold risk, as the genre was popular but not to the level it is today and doing something without established comic book characters could've proven to be a mistake. The end result was 2004's The Incredibles , which was a massive hit that grossed over $600 million at the worldwide box office.

With no prior knowledge of Mr. Incredible, Elastigirl, or any of the other characters, going into The Incredibles meant you had to pay close attention throughout the movie. The way the filmmakers made us care about this entire new group of characters was expertly done. The Incredibles remains one of Pixar's best movies and the long-awaited sequel from 2018 was another rousing success. Just getting to experience something original again that worked so well is a perfect way to spend your time.

The most popular superhero in the world is pretty easily Spider-Man. To date, we have had so many iterations of the web-slinger to love, from multiple live-action versions to fantastic animated takes to some of the best modern video games. Even through all of those projects, so many people still widely consider 2004's Spider-Man 2 to be the greatest movie ever released starring the titular character and for good reason.

Tobey Maguire delivers his best performance as Peter Parker, Alfred Molina is game as Otto Octavius (which is why both were brought back for Spider-Man: No Way Home ), and Sam Raimi does some of his best work as a director in this classic. I would love nothing more than to get the chance to see Spider-Man battle Doc Ock on the train tracks and then stop the train in one of the most perfect superhero moments ever depicted. Spider-Man 2 is a truly special film.

As noted, superhero movies broke out in a big way during the 2000s, but it wasn't until 2008 that The Dark Knight took things to the next level. A sequel to Batman Begins , this Christopher Nolan sequel expanded on what worked in that film in every single way. Christian Bale's Batman was again strong, but it was Heath Ledger's Joker that stole the show, earning the actor a posthumous Academy Award win for Best Supporting Actor.

The Dark Knight became the first superhero movie to gross $1 billion and receive Best Picture consideration at the Oscars. It made people understand how great the genre could be. Watching that unfold, from Ledger's performance to Aaron Eckhart's effort in bringing Two-Face to life and everything in between, was one of those things you had to be there for to grasp why it was such a big deal. It also would be great to see Nolan's first true blockbuster come to life for the first time.

Are there other superhero movies from the 2000s you'd like to see again for the first time? Discuss it in the comments!

articles.content:
For Alyce Tzue , reimagining Cinderella meant giving its stepsisters the chance to shape their own happily-ever-after. Netflix ’s animated adventure film Steps , co-directed with John Ripa , casts Lilith ( Ali Wong ) and Margot ( Stephanie Hsu ) as Asian immigrants in a French-inspired fairytale kingdom, where questions of belonging and privilege shape their search for happiness. Meanwhile, Cinderella ( Amanda Seyfried ) must also learn to confront her own societal complacency and dismantle stereotypes that her inherently kind nature unintentionally upholds. Here with Deadline, Tzue discusses the film’s unique visual style, reworking a traditional fairytale and bringing in new “punk rock” dimensions. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories News Bono Bowl Review: U2 Delivers Halftime Goods & Hits On Netflix & NFL's First Thanksgiving Eve Game, With A Little Help From Dolly Parton News Amanda Seyfried Admits She "Told A Lot Of People" About Her 'You Can See Everything' Role: "I'm The Most Indiscreet Person"

ALYCE TZUE: It began when Riki Lindhome and Kate Micucci had the idea for the stepsisters’ perspective and pitched it to Amy Poehler’s company, Paper Kite, which then brought it to Netflix. When I came on board, I made the stepsisters Asian immigrants to a fairytale world. We started with these pillars and bigger concepts that we wanted to honor.

One was these outsider sisters who don’t fit into the box of what you would traditionally see as a protagonist getting their happily-ever-after. That does involve race, but also the traditional feminine archetype that’s super soft-spoken and polite, sings to animals, is pretty, and has that face shape you see in every animated movie. We wanted them to find their unique happily-ever-after.

There was another idea where we wanted to speak about magic as privilege. Of course, Cinderella has gone through a lot of hardship, but you can also ask, “Well, other people in this world have gone through hardship, too. Why is it this one girl who’s elevated above everyone else and has a fairy godmother, a magic dress and all of that?” That was another concept we wanted to speak to.

DEADLINE: I want to talk more about the Asian immigrant aspect. From a cultural aspect, what did you want to showcase the most?

TZUE: I grew up in a small town in Jersey, and I was the only Asian kid in my class. It was a very homogenous white community. I was not only the artist, quiet and nerdy, but I also just felt different. Back then, you couldn’t really quite put it into words. You just felt like, “OK, the stories I had to tell and the way that I dress and the way that I understand the world is just different.”

I wanted the stepsisters to be these immigrants to a fairytale world who don’t fit the archetype, and the kingdom is full of conformists. The writers and my directing partner, John Ripa, really pushed toward the idea of a blended family where things might seem great at first, but then the world gets in the way.

The world treats difference with fear. Lilith embraces her culture in the beginning, but then when she’s rejected, especially after she shares this very deeply cultural story about the snake lady, she rejects her culture as well. You see very little cultural influence in her costumes in the middle of the movie, but then, through the love of both her sisters, she learns self-acceptance, and you actually see the snake motif return at the end. It reflects my own journey of, “OK, I’m rejected, so I reject parts of myself.” Then, as an adult, there’s this embracing of my roots and my culture again. One way is through this movie, to show how beautiful it is.

DEADLINE: There are a lot of distinct animation and personality styles happening between Lilith, Margot and Cinderella. How did you go about developing this?

TZUE: We always knew that the character styles would be really, really distinct. We wanted to make Cinderella our own, but she’s definitely inspired by classic princesses, whether from Disney or from a lot of the fairytales we had read about. We loved the French version of Cinderella by Charles Perrault, so her style is very French, and the kingdom is very French-inspired.

Lilith and Margot are both contemporary. We wanted the world to be stuck in a historical period to represent, “Oh, these are the old fairytales.” Lilith is inspired by punk rock like Emei, a Chinese American artist who wrote “The Understudy” with Justin Tranter and Olivia Rodrigo, who we have as a needle drop. Margot is also super eccentric and contemporary in that way. She geeks out on frogs, but she probably would’ve liked manga if it had existed back then. These sisters were really fun because we wanted them to be super relatable from the get-go.

DEADLINE: What was the biggest creative challenge in terms of putting the movie together? blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

TZUE: The creative challenge, honestly, was how much to include from the canon and how much to break the Cinderella story. One canon moment that gave us so much trouble is actually the stepfather’s death. For Cinderella to be orphaned, you have to kill off the father, but to show them getting together, you have to show the father. The interesting thing is that, from this story’s perspective, you want to be with Lilith the whole time. You want to sympathize with her; you want to show how the world is rejecting her. But the moment you kill off Cinderella’s father, you shift your sympathies toward her. How do you stay mad at Cinderella when her dad just died?

That montage, when you see the girls go from being kids to adults, starts right after Lilith is shut in the storm drain and ends when she becomes an adult. You wouldn’t believe how many times we swapped those events around. There were 20 different versions of that at every screening. It’s kind of surprising, a little puzzle piece that you have to treat with a sort of lightness so it doesn’t shift perspective too much.

DEADLINE: That’s interesting to me, because I was wondering how you would put it together. He dies, and then the stepmom is supposed to be “evil,” but it doesn’t go that way at all. I would have figured that that whole part of the story would be the hardest.

TZUE: Right, she’s not evil, she’s just depressed. We actually did have iterations that explored the stepmother being evil because that’s canon, but it really took a lot of the spotlight away from the sisters. Then you have to dive into, “Oh, it’s because of the mom’s influence that the stepsisters treat Cinderella this way.” That took a lot of real estate and time from the film. To get Lilith driving the story, I think we needed to focus on her and Cinderella.

DEADLINE: What was your favorite moment from the film that made you say: “I can’t believe we did it”?

TZUE: The ending. You know what all the emotions are driving to. I have a personal proof of whether or not a moment is good enough, especially something as important as the ending. If I find myself actually jumping up and down and dancing around the house like, hallelujah, this huge breakthrough moment, if I have a physical, emotional reaction like that, then I’m like, “OK, we got something.”

I’m talking about going back in time to the storm drain. And then even after that, the ripple effect of kindness. What that real act of kindness enables the world to do, and where that leads, is a huge breakthrough for us. If we didn’t have that anchor, I think things would still shift for longer. We would still be trying to find the right ending.

DEADLINE: Let’s get into the cast. You have a stacked cast. Let’s talk about Ali Wong and Stephanie Hsu and then Amanda Seyfried.

TZUE: Let me start with Ali, she’s been attached for a long while. She was the first one to join, and it was a no-brainer. We knew that Lilith had to have a spiky exterior, be hilarious and witty, and have a contemporary flavor. Ali Wong was our dream casting, so we went out to her and her only. She brought so much commentary on society and a mature take on a character who’s kind of like, “I hate this kingdom. I can see that they’re biased against me, and I totally get it. I’m going to make jokes about how the prince has been engaged to his fifth cousin since he was born.”

Then we have Amanda Seyfried, who is just incredible. We valued her so much because she takes on roles and immediately humanizes them. It’s hard for her to take on a role and make it one-dimensional. With Cinderella, especially as a legendary, iconic fairy-tale character, we needed someone who could give her many layers and allow us to sympathize with her as a fully human person. That involves her trauma, her own walls, and her people-pleasing. I thought Amanda delivered amazingly on that front. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

And Stephanie Hsu can do it all. She’s so versatile, and I want her in more comedic roles because Margot is such a boisterous, effusive wild child. Stephanie had a lot of fun with it.

DEADLINE: Young Mazino’s character is a cute, emo troll. Can you talk about his journey into the story?

TZUE: Once we broke the Cinderella story, we wanted to have a lot of fun with the idea that we had broken out of the constraints of traditional storytelling and were in a fantasy world outside the kingdom. We asked, “What other fairytale tropes could we play with?” The trolls under the bridge were interesting, and we wanted to have more action in the movie. So because of that, we have this society of trolls that don’t belong in either world, sort of like Lilith. We asked, “Can we make a character who resonates with her predicament, in that he also has emotional walls? Can you physicalize it? Can it be a literal mech that he’s in, like, ‘Oh, I don’t belong, so I’m going to protect myself in an actual mechanical creature’?” That’s where Gef came along.

We also wanted to make him super unattractive in his troll society, but beauty’s in the eye of the beholder. For humans, he’s super hunky and hot. We have so many talented writers. In the writers’ room, we were spitballing, and people laughed a lot at the idea of a super-hot troll. That’s where we got Gef from, and Young Mazino was perfect because Ali recommended him. We needed someone who had deadpan humor and a deep, monotone voice.

DEADLINE: And you’ve got Daniel Radcliffe as well. You mentioned earlier that it was a challenge of where to stay or stray from the Cinderella lore. How did you all decide to create The Prince?

TZUE: The Prince is a great opportunity to poke fun at some of the holes in the original story. One of the biggest ones was, “Well, how do you dance with a girl so close and then completely forget what she looks like, so much so that you have to fit a slipper on every woman’s foot in the kingdom?” That’s why we play with the idea of face blindness.

We knew we had to make him a little dumb, so we needed an actor who earns your sympathy above all else. The Prince is so charming and really shows you that he’s trying his best, but isn’t the sharpest tool in the toolbox. We were so lucky to get Daniel Radcliffe. He’s very picky with his roles, but he knocks it out of the park.

DEADLINE: What were some directorial inspirations you drew from, either in style or in how you shaped the story?

TZUE: We pulled inspiration from quite a few live-action films. I personally love Joe Wright's Pride and Prejudice . He tackles the intimacy of sisters so well. Some of those closer camera angles when the sisters are bonding, the rack focuses from one girl to the other, a lot of the lighting on the streets—anything that feels romantic. We also drew from movies like Little Women by Greta Gerwig and Marie Antoinette by Sofia Coppola, which was a big one as well, because she infused the Rococo era with a lot of contemporary flavor and made the whole movie feel so delicious, from the pastries and colors to the pastels. We wanted to go maximalist, and that movie gave us a lot of inspiration.

articles.title: One of the Best Thanksgiving Scenes in Movie History Happens in a Cult '90s Sequel
articles.summary: Thanksgiving movies usually have a pretty familiar routine. Somebody cooks the turkey, relatives have spirited discussion over dinner, and eventually everyone remembers they're supposed to be grateful for something. It's a perfectly nice tradition. And then there's the version where a summer camp full of spoiled children gets an unexpected history lesson and the whole […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Thanksgiving movies usually have a pretty familiar routine. Somebody cooks the turkey, relatives have spirited discussion over dinner, and eventually everyone remembers they're supposed to be grateful for something. It's a perfectly nice tradition. And then there's the version where a summer camp full of spoiled children gets an unexpected history lesson and the whole place nearly burns to the ground. That's what happens in Addams Family Values , and honestly, I don't think Thanksgiving cinema has ever quite recovered.

Ah, the Addams family … Christina Ricci was already terrific as Wednesday Addams, but the 1993 sequel gave her one of the funniest scenes of her career. She's sent to Camp Chippewa with her brother Pugsley, where the counselors have decided that putting on a Thanksgiving pageant will be a wonderful bonding experience. Wednesday isn't exactly known for embracing group activities. Things get considerably worse when she's handed a costume and expected to celebrate a version of American history that doesn't tell the whole story. The result is one of those rare comedy scenes that gets funnier every time you watch it.

Wednesday and Pugsley arrive at Camp Chippewa and immediately find themselves surrounded by the sort of cheerful children who probably think wearing matching sweaters counts as a personality. The camp's popular girls run the place, and Wednesday has absolutely no interest in joining their little social club. Then comes the Thanksgiving pageant. Amanda Buckman gets to play Sarah Miller, the beautiful pilgrim girl, while Wednesday is cast as Pocahontas. Pugsley gets to be a turkey. I'm not sure what he did to deserve that particular indignity, but it certainly doesn't help matters. The production begins with the usual sanitized version of the first Thanksgiving. The pilgrims welcome the Native Americans, everyone gets along, and apparently nobody involved has ever opened a history book. Wednesday initially plays along. Then she decides she's had enough.

What follows is ludicrous. Ricci delivers Wednesday's speech with the same wonderfully blank expression she brings to practically everything. She explains a different perspective on what happened to Indigenous people while pointing out the rather comfortable future awaiting the descendants of the pilgrims. Amanda's character has no idea what's coming. Neither do the adults sitting in the audience. Wednesday eventually announces that she intends to scalp Sarah Miller and burn the village to the ground. Then the other outcast campers join her rebellion. The set goes up in flames, the counselors lose control, and the parents suddenly discover that their children's little school play has become something considerably more exciting. It's a ridiculous scene, but that's exactly why it works. Wednesday doesn't need to shout or make some grand emotional declaration. She simply decides the play is over. And nobody is going to stop her.

Part of the reason the sequence has lasted so long is that it gives Wednesday exactly the kind of situation she was born to disrupt. The Addams family has always been funny because it sees the world differently from everyone else. What other people consider normal strikes them as deeply strange. Wednesday takes that idea and applies it to a Thanksgiving pageant that presents a very comfortable version of American history. The joke isn't simply that she's an angry little girl who wants to burn down a summer camp. She's also the only person on that stage willing to question what everybody else is celebrating. Screenwriter Paul Rudnick understood how much comedy could come from that contrast. Barry Sonnenfeld gives the sequence plenty of room to build, and Ricci never loses Wednesday's wonderfully deadpan delivery. Even the little musical cue from the original Addams Family television series makes the rebellion feel like a proper family tradition. It's hard to imagine Morticia being disappointed.

There's also something particularly satisfying about seeing the camp's social hierarchy collapse. Amanda and her friends have spent their time treating the other children as outsiders. Now those same children are running the show. Wednesday doesn't suddenly become a friendly camp counselor or learn the importance of making new friends. Thank goodness for that. She's still Wednesday. The difference is that she has found a situation where her particular brand of hostility is surprisingly useful. And the scene has only become more relevant as audiences have revisited the film over the years. Its influence even carried over into Netflix's Wednesday , which revisited the character's infamous hatred of pilgrims and included several references to the 1993 film. That's quite an achievement for a sequence that occupies only a few minutes of a 1993 comedy sequel. Plenty of movies have tried to make Thanksgiving memorable. Addams Family Values managed it by letting Wednesday Addams take over the holiday. But that might not be something to be thankful for.

EXCLUSIVE: Netflix will not be returning to the murky underworld of Amsterdam Empire.

Deadline understands that a second season of the Dutch series starring Famke Janssen is not currently planned due to scheduling issues.

Amsterdam Empire launched two years ago and is one of the streamer's most high-profile shows to come out of the Benelux region.

X-Men and GoldenEye star Janssen, who also exec produced, played Betty Jonkers, the former pop star wife of a coffee-shop mogul who has spent his life fighting against criminals, competitors and Dutch laws to become the biggest of them all. articles.title: After Three Decades, Essence Music Festival Bids Farewell to New Orleans
articles.summary: New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno teased that on Dec. 9 the city will announce details about a new “world-class” festival dedicated to Black American culture.
articles.content:
The Essence Festival of Culture, a fixture in New Orleans that has celebrated Black American culture for more than 30 years, is leaving the Big Easy.

Festival organizers and Essence Communications, which founded the annual event, announced Tuesday across their social media platforms that Essence Fest will relocate next year. The statement did not give a reason for the decision or mention where the festival was moving to. It mostly expressed gratitude to the city and its residents for helping grow the event over the years.

“You didn't simply host us. The multiday festival takes place around the Fourth of July weekend and draws major musical acts. Usher, Megan Thee Stallion and Janet Jackson are among the many performers who have headlined in recent years.

On the same day of the Essence announcement, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno teased that on Dec. 9 the city will announce details about a new “world-class” festival dedicated to Black American culture.

“Ultimately, we are working to team up with some of this country’s top Black producers to essentially bring in a festival that 1) realizes how important it is to be in the city of New Orleans and that the city of New Orleans itself is a draw,” Moreno said in a social media video. “We need to make sure that there’s widespread benefit for our local businesses, particularly our local Black businesses.”

The Essence Festival was launched in 1995 as the Essence Music Festival when Essence magazine staged a concert event in New Orleans to mark the publication's 25th anniversary. The festival has also become a political draw with panels focused on politics and voter mobilization. Politicians, both Black and white, who are in the middle of big campaigns have made Essence Fest a stop. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris spoke there in 2024 during the presidential campaign.

The Rev. Al Sharpton, founder and president of National Action Network, has participated in every festival since it began in 1995. The civil rights leader said he was saddened that such a cultural institution was leaving New Orleans but pledged continued support.

“My commitment to ESSENCE is not contingent on its geography," Sharpton said in a statement Wednesday. "Wherever the Festival lands, I will be there.”

According to a report Essence released earlier this month, the festival generated $1.3 billion in economic impact from 2022 through 2025. It also supported 11,000 jobs and led to $179.3 million in tax revenue.

However, local businesses and residents have questioned how much the festival benefits the community. During the festival, a “Clean Zone” ordinance prohibits smaller events in certain areas unless they are authorized.

A legal dispute arose in 2023 when a Black-owned bookstore and coffee shop sought to host an event promoting Black authors during the festival. The business and Essence organizers later resolved the dispute.

A similar incident occurred in 2022 when Spotify and a New Orleans real estate developer wanted to put on an event at a music club. Essence dropped the lawsuit the following year, according to NOLA.com.

articles.title: A Forgotten X-Men TV Movie Almost Gave Marvel a Different Live-Action Universe in the '90s
articles.summary: Before the MCU made its march to the top of the Hollywood mountain, Fox and Marvel Films were just starting to dip their toes into the water with an X-Men live-action TV movie. One of the ideas involved a group of lesser-known teen mutants who were not exactly household names, and the result was a […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Before the MCU made its march to the top of the Hollywood mountain, Fox and Marvel Films were just starting to dip their toes into the water with an X-Men live-action TV movie. One of the ideas involved a group of lesser-known teen mutants who were not exactly household names, and the result was a 1996 TV movie that took an interesting approach to the comics. Not only did it assemble a list of comic book fan favorites with a few surprises, but its version of Xavier's School for Gifted Youngsters looked awfully familiar to anybody who checked out the X-Men movies a decade later.

That film was Generation X , and it was never meant to be a one-off novelty. Fox and its creative team had grander plans. If the film was popular enough, it could spawn a TV series or even a handful of additional TV movies. That didn't happen, but the film still provides us with a rather intriguing glimpse of a very different road Marvel's live-action heroes might have gone down. Consider Generation X one of the earliest attempts to bring the X-Men into live-action television beyond their animated adventures.

When Generation X premiered on Fox on February 20, 1996, it was a daring project, to say the least. This made-for-television film, produced by Fox, Marvel Films, and New World Entertainment, was based on Marvel's comic-book series by the same name, and a spin-off Marvel's X-Men comic book series . It portrayed a version of America that was less than welcoming to those born with the X-gene. The government enacted the Mutant Control Act, declaring that these individuals were mutants rather than citizens and requiring them to register and report to internment camps. Not exactly the warm welcome they were probably hoping for when they were still trying to figure out what their powers could do. Xavier's School for Gifted Youngsters provided a number of those mutants with a place to learn what they could do and what it all meant.

The plot follows a group of young mutants learning to control their unusual abilities at Xavier's School for Gifted Youngsters. It's there where they find a place to belong in a world that fears them. Their attempts to adjust to life at the school take an unexpected turn when a mysterious scientist named Russell Tresh begins targeting mutants for his own experiments. It's a story about friendship, acceptance, and the challenges of growing up different, with a distinctly 1990s superhero twist.

Overall, I think the casting was pretty good. Heather McComb played Jubilee. Amarilis was given the role of Monet St. Croix, aka M, and Agustin Rodriguez played Skin. Suzanne Davis was Buff, Randall Slavin was Refrax, and Bumper Robinson was Mondo. Finola Hughes played Emma Frost, Jeremy Ratchford played Sean Cassidy, aka Banshee, and Matt Frewer was Russell Tresh. I also thought that considering it was an 87-minute TV movie with a $4 million price tag, that is an impressive lineup of Marvel characters and actors. Fox and its production partners must have been hoping the comics and the X-Men Saturday morning cartoon would give them a head start in hooking viewers along. If enough folks showed up, there was room to do much more with them.

One of the more interesting things about Generation X was just how much the production had to revise its comic-book roster. Some characters simply weren't possible with the effects the TV movie had to offer. Executive producer and screenwriter Eric Blakeney told the Los Angeles Times that Chamber was too cost-prohibitive because of the constant energy effect on his chest and lower face. Other characters didn't make the final version. A retrospective named Chamber, Husk, and Synch among the omissions, while Penance's complicated backstory was too involved for a first appearance. Instead, Buff and Refrax were new additions to the team. Screenwriter Eric Blakeney developed the characters, with Scott Lobdell potentially contributing their names.. The production even suggested they could be incorporated into the comics if people liked them. Sadly, Buff and Refrax never made it into the comics and only exists in the TV show.

The film also found an oddball villain in Russell Tresh, played by Matt Frewer. Tresh was a scientist who had once worked with Emma Frost before becoming an underhanded advertising pitchman. He'd invented a device that allowed him to enter the dream dimension, and he was out to capture a brain cell from one of the young mutants for his experiments. Good way to complicate a teenager's experience at school. There was plenty of mutating going on with the cast, but underneath it all, Generation X was still basically an X-Men story : misfits with strange abilities in a world afraid of things it doesn't understand. Unfortunately, the film never received the follow-up Fox had hoped for. No TV series, no additional TV movies, just a four-year gap until X-Men finally opened in theaters and changed everything. It's fun to speculate about what might have happened with this odd little experiment.

What do you think about this little-known TV show? Let us know if you think it's still worth watching and if you like Generation X!

American actor-director Mario Van Peebles (“New Jack City”), Oscar-nominated Mauritanian filmmaker Abderrahmane Sissako (“Timbuktu”), Nigerian filmmaker Kunle Afolayan (“Aníkúlápó”) and French actor-director Jean-Pascal Zadi (“Simply Black”) are among the industry figures set to attend the fourth edition of Ivory Coast’s International Salon for Audiovisual Content of Abidjan ( SICA ).

The gathering comes amid considerable upheaval in Africa’s media landscape. Pay-TV subscriptions in sub-Saharan Africa fell 2.8% to 33.2 million in 2025, according to research firm Omdia. Following its acquisition of South African pay-TV operator MultiChoice in September 2025, French media group Canal+ shut down MultiChoice’s streaming platform Showmax in April, citing financial losses.

At SICA, a panel on adapting to streaming platforms and new distribution models will bring together representatives of Ivorian networks RTI, NCI, A+ Ivoire, Life TV and 7info alongside Netflix and broadcasters from Senegal, Cameroon, Benin and Canada. A separate discussion will examine how regulation can strengthen the market for local content on national television channels.

The theatrical sector, meanwhile, offers encouraging signs. According to the European Audiovisual Observatory’s Focus 2026 report, national film releases in Anglophone West Africa doubled from 58 in 2024 to 117 in 2025, with Nollywood’s regional market share rising from 46% to 50%. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Mobilizing capital to sustain local production will be central to SICA’s program this year. Producer Virginie Besson-Silla (“ Lucy ”), distributor Claire Diao and Meta’s Balkissa Idé Siddo will join Ivory Coast’s Minister of Culture and Francophonie Françoise Remarck for a panel titled “The Creative Economy: Financing, Production and Distribution.”

Besson-Silla and Idé Siddo will also be part of a panel with Ivorian filmmaker Philippe Lacôte (“Night of the Kings”) and representatives of financial institutions, including the African Export-Import Bank, to discuss financing Africa’s creative economy.

A memorandum of understanding aimed at facilitating financing of the audiovisual sector is set to be signed between Ivory Coast’s Agency for Media Support and Development and the commercial NSIA Banque Côte d’Ivoire, while in a masterclass, Sissako and South African producer Joel Phiri will tackle financing and co-production in challenging contexts.

SICA’s pitching competition, with Besson-Silla and Zadi as its patrons, will span film, television series, documentaries, animation and student projects. Running alongside the competition, the SICA Business Hub, launched last year, will connect African audiovisual creators and producers with international broadcasters, distributors, buyers and investors.

With Japan as this year’s country of honor, Kazuki Sunami of CoMix Wave Films, the animation studio behind Makoto Shinkai’s “ Your Name ” and “Suzume,” will deliver the inaugural conference address. Japanese media specialist Masayoshi Isago will join Ivorian filmmakers Abel Kouamé and Adja Soro for a discussion on animation, while digital entertainment specialist Masato Tanaka will participate in SICA Campus, the market’s educational program for students.

Congolese animation and visual effects specialist Sidney Kombo-Kintombo and Van Peebles will deliver keynotes on Africa’s creative economy and cultural diplomacy, respectively, with dedicated sessions exploring animation, VFX, gaming and emerging technologies.

Afolayan, Senegalese broadcaster 7TV’s Maïmouna Faye and Ivorian producer Charly Kodjo will explore ways to strengthen South-South cooperation. Discussions on the final day will focus on Africa-Asia partnerships and how film and television can strengthen Africa’s global profile. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

In Ivory Coast, where cinema admissions surpassed 400,000 in 2025, according to the Ministry of Communication, connecting local productions with domestic audiences remains a challenge. American films accounted for 82% of admissions in 2024, compared with just 6% for Ivorian films, according to the country’s National Film Office.

Accordingly, seeking to engage a wider audience, the parallel SICA OFF program runs Nov. 25-Dec. 6, with Sissako serving as patron of its opening ceremony. It features a Japanese film festival opening with “Your Name,” premieres including Sissako’s immersive film “Artou” and Ivorian-Congolese production “Naïké,” and heritage screenings of Van Peebles’ “Baadasssss!” and a newly restored copy of Henri Duparc’s 1972 Ivorian drama “Abusuan.”

More than 100 screenings will be offered at a reduced ticket price of 2,000 CFA Francs ($3.50) from Dec. 2-6 to encourage cinema attendance.

Van Peebles will serve as patron of the market’s closing ceremony, featuring a tribute to Ivorian cinema pioneer Timité Bassori, the SICA d’Or awards recognizing excellence in television programming and presenting, and the pitching competition awards.

articles.title: 'Chhota Bheem' Creator and 'Black Warrant' Publisher Weigh Book-to-Screen Economics at WAVES Film Bazaar
articles.summary: Streaming has changed how Indian authors write, and a screen option can pay a writer more than several editions of a book ever will, publishers, producers and creators said during a panel at WAVES Film Bazaar, the market of the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa. The session, "From Print to Pixel: The […]
articles.content:
Streaming has changed how Indian authors write, and a screen option can pay a writer more than several editions of a book ever will, publishers, producers and creators said during a panel at WAVES Film Bazaar , the market of the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa.

The session, "From Print to Pixel: The Transmedia Paradigm," was moderated by journalist Mayank Shekhar. On stage were Priya Kapoor, editorial director of Roli Books; South African filmmaker Tarina Patel, founder and CEO of Tarina P Productions; Rajiv Chilaka, founder and managing director of Green Gold Animation; Raghav Chandra, a retired Indian Administrative Service officer, novelist and founder director of the Bhopal Literature and Art Festival; and Prakash Magdum, former managing director of the National Film Development Corp. (NFDC). blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories 'Hazara Town' Review: A Restrained but Deeply Affecting Doc Portrait of an Afghan Refugee Family Living in Limbo Motorhead’s Classic ‘Orgasmatron’ Gets a Mighty 40th Anniversary Sonic Upgrade and Deluxe Edition: Album Review

Kapoor, who has commissioned and edited titles including " Black Warrant ," "Dongri to Dubai" and "Taj Mahal Foxtrot," said that since streamers arrived in India, writers have become aware their books can travel beyond the page.

"We definitely get submissions where you read it and you know that somebody is 100% thinking of a film adaptation, and others who are writing because they had a book in mind," Kapoor said.

Production houses and directors in Mumbai call Roli from time to time with briefs that track the trends – a young adult story, say, or mythology, which is in vogue now. A while back, they wanted hard-hitting non-fiction.

Then there are writers who have already optioned or sold a screen story and come to Roli for a book version, because the deal needs underlying IP. "It's essentially a screenplay that's been summarized into a book, and that is where the trouble begins," Kapoor said. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"Black Warrant" took a far less conventional route. Former warden Sunil Gupta, recently retired from Delhi's Tihar jail, walked into Kapoor's office with Praveen Jain, a former chief photographer at The Indian Express, and spent an hour telling stories. Gupta couldn't write, so a legal intern named Satyabhan recorded and transcribed sessions built on Kapoor's questions, and Sunetra Choudhury, author of the prison book "Behind Bars," came on board as co-writer. The chapters followed the way Gupta remembered events rather than any episodic plan, though the show's writers later told Kapoor the structure suited them.

Gupta, the protagonist of both book and series, is very happy with the result, Kapoor said. "He goes for the shooting also, he goes for the premieres, he's a star." He made a point of flagging scenes that never happened, and Kapoor has told him the filmmakers are allowed those creative liberties.

The money gap between the two industries is wide. In Indian English-language publishing, Kapoor put a bestseller at 5,000 copies, and a hit adaptation does not change that much. "Our reading audience is not our watching, viewing audience," she said. A screen deal, though, can pay an author more than five or 10 editions of a book would, even when the project never gets made.

Chilaka's " Chhota Bheem " took the opposite path, starting on TV and spreading outward. The character borrows only the strength of Bheem from the Mahabharata, transplanted into an ordinary village kid. Over 18 years, Green Gold has made more than 1,000 episodes, over 100 TV features, around five feature films and four spinoffs, with some 2,000 characters and more than 1,000 licensed products. Chilaka put the business done on the property at more than INR10 billion ($112 million).

The Netflix spinoff "Mighty Little Bheem," which reimagines the hero as a baby, is among the streamer's top preschool shows internationally, Chilaka said. Green Gold made it without dialogue. "So we gambled with that, and the gamble paid off," he said. The show also leaves out Bheem's father, which Chilaka said drew a strong response from single-mother households in North and South America.

Coming next year is "Sing with Bheem," a musical spinoff series. A stage musical bowed last month at the Royal Opera House in Mumbai, a Chhota Bheem cafe is open in Hyderabad with seven or eight more planned across India, and the character has fronted public campaigns in West Bengal, Chhattisgarh and on Western Railways. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The franchise grew out of insecurity, Chilaka said. Green Gold was a 20- to 30-person studio making an animated "Krishna" while 17 other studios worked on their own Krishna projects. It sold the film to Cartoon Network, but animation budgets never covered production costs, so Chilaka planned for home video, comics, merchandise and birthday parties from the start, and modeled his ensemble on "Friends" so every child could find a match.

"Sustaining is still okay, we've done it for 18 years, but getting another hit like that is the biggest challenge because we've done so well," Chilaka said.

Patel, whose credits include "Mandela's Gun," has mostly built films from firsthand accounts rather than books. Her current project is a real-life story set against boxing and apartheid, for which she optioned what she judged the best of five or six books on the subject. Announcing it brought out a string of claimants waving documents, followed by a long, stressful stretch with entertainment lawyers.

"If it's a public figure, anyone can tell the story. Irrespective of whether there's a family, there's an estate, their books, anyone is entitled to tell the story of a public figure," Patel said. Diaries, personal photographs and other private family material still require access, she added.

Chandra said the Bhopal festival, now eight editions old, programs a session or two on literature to cinema each year, with past editions covering "12th Fail," "Bandit Queen" and "The Railway Men." He pointed to universality and contemporary relevance as what carries a book to the screen. His own novels, "Scent of a Game" and "Kali's Daughter," drew interest from a prominent director just before COVID that went nowhere. At the session he showed an AI-generated pitch deck built from a "Scent of a Game" subplot about the last wild cheetahs in India, put together by a junior colleague in about 15 minutes.

Magdum, who headed the National Film Archive of India during Mahatma Gandhi's 150th birth anniversary, has been mining archival footage of Gandhi for a book, Shekhar said. Magdum recalled how Fox Movietone crews hauled sound equipment by bullock cart to a Gujarat village to film Gandhi with sync sound shortly after India's first talkie, "Alam Ara," opened on March 14, 1931. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"A book is a very private kind of a thing. You are imagining in your own world whatever is the writer creating," Magdum said, adding that an adaptation works when the director captures the soul of what the writer meant.

Asked for their favorite book-to-screen adaptations, Magdum and Patel both picked "Slumdog Millionaire," drawn from Vikas Swarup's novel "Q&A." Patel, a friend of Swarup's, said he wrote it while posted in Cape Town and that screenwriter Simon Beaufoy's love story turned it around. Chandra chose "Omkara" and "The Guide," Chilaka the "Harry Potter" and "The Lord of the Rings" films, and Kapoor "The English Patient."

articles.content:
Seven of India's JioStar television channels, including popular Hindi-language entertainment channels Star Plus and Colors, are now streaming in the U.S. on live TV service Fubo .

Alongside Star Plus and Colors, the slate comprises Star Bharat, Colors Rishtey, Colors Cineplex, MTV India and English-language news channel News18 English.

The four general entertainment channels carry both fiction and non-fiction programming. Their libraries include popular dramas "Kyunki Saas Bhi Kabhi Bahu Thi," "Anupama" and "Yeh Rishta Kya Kehlata Hai," as well as reality franchises " Bigg Boss ," "India Ke Top 1 Percent" and "Laughter Chefs." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Alanis Morissette Blends Theatrical Sketches, Memoir Talk and Massive Hits in Captivating 'Butterfly With a Machete' Residency: Concert Review 'Ghost Soldier' Review: Jim Caviezel Is a Superheroic Soldier in an Uninspired, Retrograde Actioner

Colors Cineplex is the group's movie channel, programming Hindi films that range from older Bollywood favorites to hits such as "Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham," "Tiger 3," "Welcome" and "Dil Toh Pagal Hai." MTV India adds its youth-skewing formats "Roadies," "Splitsvilla" and "Hustle," while News18 English covers news out of India.

Viewers can get the channels through two Fubo packs. The Hindi Entertainment & Cricket pack costs $34.99 for the first month as an introductory offer, rising to $39.99 a month after that. The JioStar pack is priced at $10.99 a month.

Amit Malhotra, head of international business at JioStar, said: "The opportunity for Indian entertainment internationally is no longer limited to taking individual shows or channels overseas. It is about building a distribution ecosystem through which the breadth of Indian television can travel. At JioStar, our approach is to bring the full spectrum of our content, from fiction and reality to cinema and youth entertainment, to South Asian families in the U.S. and to a wider audience who can connect with it." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

JioStar is pitching the move at the South Asian diaspora, for whom Indian TV is still a close tie to Indian culture, and also at a wider audience curious about the country's storytelling.

Malhotra added that the Fubo launch gives JioStar a solid base in the U.S. as it puts together a broader international distribution network for its linear channels.

articles.title: 'South Park' Season Finale Drops Kenny Into 'Grand Theft Auto VI' as South America Comes Clean
articles.summary: Power outages, penis billionaires and an undead Kenny collide as the season ties up (most of) its loose ends.
articles.content:
All is not well in South America (née South Park ) in the season 29 finale. The long-anticipated November release of Grand Theft Auto VI — the show's metaphorical stand-in for the midterm elections — has finally arrived, but rolling power outages caused by local billionaires' AI-powered data centers are keeping the townspeople — from the little-seen Goth Kids to Mr. Garrison to Big Gay Al, and of course, our core boy heroes — from enjoying the biggest media release of all time.

Mass protest ensues, and we're reminded of the deep corruption that has taken hold of the Colorado town, starting with Mayor McDaniels' administration taking kickbacks from the tiny-penis billionaires — who, we'll recall, broke Butters' fight against them earlier in the season with a backroom deal to keep building their data centers in town and siphoning its power. Butters and family deliver a fun nod to "It's a Good Life," a classic Twilight Zone plot here, with Butters' parents believing he has supernatural powers and are absolutely terrified of him. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories TV 'South Park' Takes Aim at Jensen Huang, Nvidia Spy Scandal in Next Episode Business Nvidia Board Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO

For an episode that packs plenty in, calling back to much of the season's action and picking up most of the plot threads it introduced (minus, unfortunately, the great Tweek and Craig ), it's Lu Kim, the Asian American owner of City Wok and now City Ending massage, who walks away with the heaviest storyline. He's quickly scapegoated and placed under suspicious watch by armed South America residents, who are made aware of a Chinese spy that feels a little like a recent international tech world scandal. A Shitty Ending feels inevitable. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Meanwhile, Kenny, who was believed to have died in an e-bike accident in the season premiere, resurfaces terrifyingly. The boys first spot him in the distance outside; after following him, they discover he's a zombie. He points at them horrifically, à la Donald Sutherland in Invasion of the Body Snatchers , then disintegrates before their eyes. He later reemerges to haunt them in the worst place imaginable: inside Grand Theft Auto VI as the boys play. Their supposedly deceased friend exits the game as some sort of four-legged beast, ready to devour little Butters.

Whatever is going on here, our longtime elementary school heroes are going to figure it out — and in doing so, tie up all (well, most) of the season's threads. Shaken to his core by Kenny's appearance, Butters fesses up about the billionaires' earlier bribe, then tells the boys how he offloaded the data centers to Peter Mullins' house. The boys head there next and discover a high-tech data center in their classmate's never-looked-at backyard.

When the boys bring what they know about Kenny — whose spirit, they've discerned, is somehow trapped in South America — to the local police, they also lay out the billionaires' secret bribes and the town's corruption. The detectives and officers are none too surprised. As Lil' Randy points out after dramatically barging into the station, the whole town has become corrupt, and it all started with the name change to South America.

It's time for everyone to come clean: The mayor confesses to her administration's corruption at the hands of the tiny-penis billionaires, but there's no accountability for her or her office, just as there's none for Randy and the others actually involved in Kenny's death. This is South Park, after all, and it's easier to keep Lu Kim as the scapegoat. Like Nvidia's Jensen Huang , Kim is ousted here at the behest of the small-penis billionaires — he's sent off in a rocket, a South Park tradition that has spelled the demise of Ms. Ellen, Jambu the orca and, of course, Tom Cruise. By the end of the episode and the season, the core four boys of South Park Elementary are restored, Randy is still Lil' Randy, it seems, and the town, according to the iconic sign at its edge, is once again called South Park.

articles.content:
Jesse Eisenberg recently told the New Yorker that fans of his are “mostly fine” when he’s in public, a fact he attributes to his generally sexless resume.

“People are mostly fine,” he said to reporter Rachel Syme when asked if strangers ever interrupt him when they spot him working on scripts. (The "A Real Pain" actor told Syme that his typical schedule revolves around sitting at a branch of the New York Public Library, where he writes from nine to five). “It’s because there’s no sexuality to my work,” he continued. “I think once the public is asked to want to sleep with a person onscreen, that person’s life is fundamentally different.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories 'Daredevil' Star Charlie Cox Asked to Audition for James Bond but Was Told He's Too Old: 'Robert Pattinson Is the Same Age as Me!' Robert Pattinson’s 007 Announcement on Social Media Proves Amazon Is Already Changing the Bond Franchise

Though, despite Eisenberg’s assertion, his “Fleishman Is in Trouble” co-star Claire Danes told Syme that people began to “rubberneck” when the two had a coincidental run-in on the street and stopped to chat. “People are very aware of him as a figure, even though he is so determined to be invisible,” she said.

Elsewhere in the lengthy profile, Aaron Sorkin, who directed Eisenberg as a young Mark Zuckerberg in “The Social Network,” told the outlet that “I hardly know him at all,” noting that the actor reminds “me of Holden Caulfield, if that makes any sense. He has absolutely no patience for phonies.” Eisenberg earned an Oscar nomination for the part, but has since been outspoken about his decision not to reprise the role in the director's follow-up, “ The Social Reckoning ,” released earlier this year; “I’d be out at a bar, and a drunk guy would say, ‘Hey, I love your website,’” he told the New Yorker. “And as I’m pretending to laugh, I’d just wish all of the oxygen would leave my lungs, and that I would collapse on the floor in front of this guy and show him what he’s doing to me.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The actor-turned-director, who is currently promoting “ The Debut ,” his latest project, also spoke about creating “nonhierarchical” environments on his sets. “How could you be making a movie about a woman who’s an underdog, who no one notices, and then have a set where the people walking around feel like that?” he said. “You’d have to be so stupid and blind and compartmentalizing, in a psychopathic way, to write a movie about that and then perpetuate it.”

“The Debut,” Eisenberg’s third feature as a director, stars Julianne Moore as Mona Friedman, a New Jersey housewife who auditions for a part in her local theater’s production of a fictional musical. After she’s cast as Miss Danielle, Friedman’s life begins to unravel as she becomes more consumed with the role and falls under the spell of director Jerry Blankenbuehler (Paul Giamatti).

articles.summary: Marvel Studios In the run up to Avengers: Doomsday, Marvel fans have had some big questions about the highly anticipated MCU film. articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google In the run up to Avengers: Doomsday , Marvel fans have had some big questions about the highly anticipated MCU film. Those questions have spanned everything from what X-Men will appear, if the Steve Rogers we’ve seen in teasers and trailer s is actually the “real” Steve Rogers, and more, but one of the biggest has been surprisingly simple: why doesn’t Magneto just take Doom down? After all, Victor Von Doom is wearing metal armor and Magneto’s power is magnetism. Now, a brand-new teaser for Avengers: Doomsd ay is here with new footage and an answer to that question.

Released on Wednesday, the brief teaser features Sir Ian McKellan’s Magneto explaining that Doom is “pain” and “extinction” before showing the hero trying to pull Doom’s armor off of him. While Doom’s mask begins to pull away from his body, it only gets so far and is kept close by glowing green energy. Check it out for yourself below.

New teaser for ‘AVENGERS: DOOMSDAY’. In theaters December 18. pic.twitter.com/xQJvjlLsru

That glowing green energy appears to be the key to why Magneto can’t dismantle and disable Doom. The easiest explanation for what is happening here is that Doom’s armor is able to resist Magneto’s power by way of magic and that would actually make sense. While Doom’s armor is iconic, his biggest advantage is that he is a master of both science and sorcery. It makes perfect sense that Doom would be utilizing magic to defeat science — in this case, Magneto’s magnetism powers — and keep his armor in place. This gives him a pretty solid advantage over one of the most powerful of mutants and that’s bad news for the heroes. Things also don’t look especially good for the heroes on another level in the teaser, either. There’s another moment where it looks like Doom is able to simply stop (or steal) Magneto’s powers entirely. That probably isn’t good, both for Magneto specifically and the heroes writ large.

Of course, there’s something else a bit interesting about this teaser in addition to the revelation of why Magneto can’t simply stop Doom by pulling off his armor. If you look very carefully at the close up of Doom’s eyes as his mask is being pulled from him, you can somewhat see the scarring on his face. As Marvel fans know, Doctor Doom has facial scarring. Exactly how he acquired those scars varies a bit — as is the case with most comics characters, their origins shift a bit over time — as does just how extensive the scars are. But getting even a small peek at things in this teaser makes for an exciting little gem for fans — and it will be very interesting to see exactly how Avengers: Doomsday portrays the man beneath the mask in the movie.

Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters December 18 th .

Bob Iger 's compensation frustrations and an extramarital affair with an ABC employee that resulted in a pregnancy are some of the revelations laid out in an upcoming tell-all book.

The House of Mouse , written by longtime Wall Street Journal reporter Robbie Whelan, is an unauthorized biography and corporate history of the former Disney CEO that releases Dec. 1. Iger reportedly declined to be interviewed for the book.

In the book, Whelan claimed Iger had an extramarital affair with an ABC marketer in the early 1990s while he was running ABC Entertainment at the time, according to The New York Times , which obtained an advance copy. articles.title: Every Avengers Doomsday Theory & Leak Confirmed or Debunked By The Final Trailer
articles.summary: Marvel Studios Avengers: Doomsday has done a masterful job of keeping its story details, big twists, and surprise cameos all tucked safely under the veil of secrecy. But, like with any Marvel Studios film, Doomsday has had supposed "leaks" about its story and reveals bubbling in the corners of sites like Reddit since production began. Early on, […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Avengers: Doomsday has done a masterful job of keeping its story details, big twists, and surprise cameos all tucked safely under the veil of secrecy. But, like with any Marvel Studios film, Doomsday has had supposed "leaks" about its story and reveals bubbling in the corners of sites like Reddit since production began. Early on, it was easy for Marvel to play the quiet denial game of simply letting rumors fly; as more and more official footage and promotional materials for Avengers: Doomsday get released, that secrecy gets harder to maintain.

After every new Avengers: Doomsday trailer , we've broken down the major leaks and rumors that look more credible. Naturally, the final trailer offers more contextual and corroborative evidence than any previous one, and if you've been keeping track of the clues, there's a lot you can soft-confirm about Doomsday at this point. Below are just a few examples.

Yep, it's true: one of the greatest heroes of The Infinity Saga is at the heart of why all realities are falling apart in The Multiverse Saga. The final Avengers: Doomsday trailer puts Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) and his Avengers: Endgame epilogue at the forefront, revealing Steve has lived at least a decade with Peggy Carter (Hayley Atwell) and is raising a son.

However, he is tracked down by Reed Richards and the Fantastic Four (and Doom?) Steve is put in an impossible position of having to answer the hero's call again, while possibly sacrificing the entire life and family he's built for himself.

One of the oldest theories about Avengers: Doomsday is all but dead now. Basically, the theory was that Avengers: Doomsday would tap into a time-honored MCU tradition of having Loki pull a fake-out illusion or impersonation: Only this time he'd be performing the role of a lifetime as Steve Rogers. The theory was that Steve Rogers has a lot to lose, and Loki doesn't fully trust Doom, so the two make a plan for Loki to let Steve and his family be tucked safely away, while he steps in as Steve to go on the quest to save the multiverse and to discern what Doom is really up to.

However, the final Avengers: Doomsday trailer makes it clear that Steve's dilemma is exactly what the emotional core of the film will be. Rogers will have to reconcile with his selfish desire, possibly dooming trillions of other lives. And the film won't let him off the hook about it easily.

They can try all the clever marketing tricks and altered shots they like, but at this point we can soft-confirm that early on in Avengers: Doomsday , Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) will exploit his history and bond with Reed Richards (Pedro Pascal) to go on the quest to "fix" the multiverse, while really executing his own plan to recreate reality.

Fantastic Four: First Steps sets up that alliance in its mid-credits scene when Doom comes to the Baxter Building; in recent interviews, RDJ, Pascal, and directors Joe and Anthony Russo have all spoken openly about Doom and Reed being friends… until they aren't . Fans have also pieced together footage from multiple trailers showing the moment when Doom turns on the heroes . You know Downey wasn't going to do something as simple as a hammy archvillain arc. Doom will have all the complexity (and screen time) he needs before Avengers: Secret Wars .

Okay, so this doesn't have anything specifically to do with Avengers: Doomsday 's Final Trailer; it definitely has to do with recent circumstances that have happened in accordance with the trailer's release, though.

The VisionQuest finale included a post-credits scene from Doomsday , revealing that Doom goes to the ruins of Wundagore Mountain and resurrects Wanda Maximoff, the Scarlet Witch (Elizabeth Olsen) . So Scarlet Witch is in Doomsday , but why haven't we seen her? Look closely again at that last trailer, because you actually did.

The "Latverian Witches" Doom has with him may be the worst-kept secret of Doomsday . We knew Wanda was one of them long before Doomsday ; Loki star Sophia Di Martino dropped major hints that Sylvie was in Doomsday over a year ago. When Marvel Studios revealed costumes for the witches and a fourth character, "Boris," fans instantly spotted a third-eye slot in the helmet and knew Doctor Strange (Benedict Cumberbatch) was behind the mask. That made Strange's last known travel companion, the sorceress Clea (played by mega-star Charlize Theron) the last witch we needed to identify. At this point, Doomsday will pull a bigger twist on us if it's not them.

One aspect of Avengers: Doomsday marketing that's not getting nearly enough attention are the scenes on Earth-616 featuring the Fantastic Four, Wakandans, and Namor's kingdom of Talokan. After making an alliance with the Avengers, it's clear some characters head over to Earth-10005 to confront the X-Men, while others remain back on Earth-616 as defense.

There are several scenes spread across the Avengers: Doomsday trailers that all indicate a major battle occurring on Earth-616. We've seen Shuri (Letitia Wright) go into full Black Panther mode alongside the Dora Milaje and M'Baku (Winston Duke); Namor (Tenoch Huerta) has been speeding through water with his battleface on, while both Ben Grimm (Ebon Moss-Bachrach) and Sue Storm (Vanessa Kirby) are seen pushing themselves to the limit. There's even a scene between Johnny Storm (Joseph Quinn) and Franklin suggesting the battle may not go well.

Early leaks about Doomsday addressed this, saying while Doom is busy manipulating an Avengers vs. X-Men situation on Earth-10005, he will also send a squad of heavy-hitters to strike at Earth-616. The rumors of who will be in that evil cabal have been all over the place; right now an evil version of Hulk (Maestro) seems likely (as does a Thing vs. Hulk slugfest), but "King Thanos," "Hydra Cap," and "Superior Iron Man" (Chris Evans and Robert Downey Jr. taking on second cameo roles) have also been rumored to show up.

Avengers: Endgame - Encore had a post-credits scene that revealed the Time Variance Authority is definitely part of the film. That confirmation came on the heels of Marvel Studios revealing an entire set piece of a destroyed TVA as part of Doomsday 's promotion, all but confirming that there will be a major showdown at the headquarters of the multiverse's police force.

Avengers: Doomsday trailers have all sidestepped the TVA connection, but that's understandable. Early leaks for the film have said the "Battle of the TVA" will be another epic surprise in the film, as the TVA is rumored to have assembled its own squad of Avengers pulled from the multiverse, which could offer any number of surprise cameos from Marvel movie stars both past and present.

You can feel it, can't you? Heck, it's even clear from the footage details that Marvel Studios is trying to hide it . Avengers: Doomsday has a massive cast, but we haven't seen everyone yet. The official cast has already added a half-dozen extra characters since the initial announcement (Hulk, Scarlet Witch, the TVA crew, Kate Bishop, Cassie Lang), and others (Deadpool, Wolverine, Spider-Man) are all but assured to be there.

There are even rumors that more legacy characters could pop up (more of the Fox X-Men or Fantastic Four actors); it's also rumored that certain actors will play variants of their own characters (like evil Iron Man and Cap). The deepest rabbit holes claim there will be a repeat of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness , with Marvel pulling some A-list celebrities in to honor longtime fan-casting wishes (a Tom Cruise Iron Man variant). It's a hard line to measure: big cameos that don't get used for Doomsday could still find their place in Secret Wars . But we know for certain after this last trailer that more characters are waiting to be revealed.

Avengers: Doomsday will be in theaters on December 18th.

articles.content:
U2 paid tribute to Dolly Parton as part of its halftime performance Wednesday night at the NFL 's first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game. The "duet" between a live Bono and a recording of Parton from last summer was the centerpiece of a highly promoted 10-minute set between halves of the contest between the Los Angeles Rams and Green Bay Packers, streamed exclusively on Netflix .

U2 did not attempt to cram as many songs into their brief performance as other superstars have during halftime performances, getting in just three. The band opened with an abridged "Sunday Bloody Sunday" and ended with "Where the Streets Have No Name" — only squeezing in one song from their new album, the Parton duet, "Torn," with images of Dolly projected onto three huge curtains that dropped around their stage at the 50-yard line. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Ceremony Gets Fired Up With Live-Wire Numbers From U2, the Chili Peppers, Usher, Cynthia Erivo, Sienna Spiro, Aerosmith and More Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Designates the Troubadour as a Landmark Venue; Going Forward, L.A. About a hundred extras took part in the performances — forming not a marching band, but a marching choir. U2 was also joined by the Womack Sisters , a vocal trio that has just been nominated for best new artist at the Grammys.

The dancers first appeared as part of "Sunday Bloody Sunday," which included an interpolation of the Supremes' "Stop in the Name of Love," rendered as something more somber, as performed by the Womack Sisters, to better fit in with U2's theme of civil war. Bono repeated the "torn" part of that early '80s anthem as a segue into the song "Torn," as he and the spectral Parton harmonized on the recent song about a family at war.
