articles.title: Peter Berg on the ‘Two Truths’ of War in ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ and the ‘Incredibly Funny’ ‘Hancock 2’ Script Will Smith Sent Him: ‘I Love Will Smith, and I Always Will’
articles.summary: Peter Berg knows what he wants from the world, and that’s peace. The 62-year-old filmmaker behind epics like “Lone Survivor” and “Deepwater Horizon” and the sports drama series “Friday Night Lights” may have made his most personal film yet with the World War II drama “The Mosquito Bowl.” He also, it turns out, has a […]
articles.content:
Peter Berg knows what he wants from the world, and that’s peace.

The 62-year-old filmmaker behind epics like “Lone Survivor” and “Deepwater Horizon” and the sports drama series “Friday Night Lights” may have made his most personal film yet with the World War II drama “ The Mosquito Bowl .” He also, it turns out, has a knack for timing.

When we spoke on Nov. 13, a global Microsoft outage had knocked Outlook offline for millions of users the day before. Berg held it up as a warning shot, proof of how little it would take for the world to go dark in a war with China. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories How to Watch 'Yellowjackets’ Season 4 Online: The Hit Thriller Returns for Its Final Season

“Your phones won't work. Your bank accounts won't work. Every system that we are depending on will shut down instantly,” he says. “What we saw was just a tiny taste of what that can feel like.”

That same afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop after a communications failure hit the country’s air traffic control centers, halting every departing flight in the United States. Then I received a text message from Berg.

“Interesting after our talk,” he wrote. “All flights grounded.”

Based on Buzz Bissinger’s 2022 book “The Mosquito Bowl: A Game of Life and Death in World War II,” the film follows a group of college football stars who joined the Marine Corps after Pearl Harbor, played a now-legendary game on Guadalcanal on Christmas Eve 1944 and landed on Okinawa months later. Many of them never came home. Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Ray Nicholson and Tom Francis lead the ensemble and Berg steps in front of the camera as Lt. Gen. Simon Buckner. After an Oct. 30 theatrical run, the film is now streaming on Netflix. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

But the biggest news Berg made has nothing to do with World War II. Flights may have been grounded, but he’s ready to get “Hancock” airborne again. Berg tells Variety that Will Smith has sent him a script for “Hancock 2,” the long-gestating sequel to their 2008 superhero hit and that he would sign on to make it.

“I don't even know if I'm supposed to say it or not, but Will sent me an incredibly funny, great script for 'Hancock 2,'” Berg says. “I would do it. The universe has to line up.”

It's the most concrete sign of life the sequel has shown in years. Talk of a follow-up has circulated since the original grossed more than $600 million worldwide, and in February 2025, Smith teased a “really cool” idea during a Twitch livestream, saying Zendaya was being approached for a role. Sony has never confirmed a sequel is in the works.

Berg also offered something close to a character reference for his star, who was banned from Academy events for 10 years after slapping Chris Rock onstage at the 2022 Oscars. Berg doesn’t mention the incident by name.

“I think the time for me is right for Will to do that role, and for many reasons,” he says. “I think Will Smith is a really good human being and a very, very talented human being and just like me and I would guess you, not a flawless human being. I'm flawed. I've made some mistakes, and I'll probably make some more. But I love Will Smith, and I always will. And I know a lot of other people do too. So if that ever happens, it would be, I think, a really special film.”

Before any return to the “Hancock” universe, Berg has another mission to finish. He's co-writing and directing Paramount's “Call of Duty” with Taylor Sheridan, set in the “Modern Warfare” universe and dated for June 30, 2028. When asked about it, he offered the only thing he could at this stage: a tease that the franchise's most famous face is likely coming along.

“We've already said that we're basing it on the 'Modern Warfare' universe,” Berg says. “So you can probably expect to see Captain Price, I would think.”

Casting is “beginning,” Berg says. He credits Paramount chief David Ellison and Activision for being “really smart about how they want to do it,” adding, “Personally, I think they hired the right two guys to help them do it.” He calls Sheridan “the best possible partner I could have in the whole world.” As for more details, he says, “Check in with me, I'd say, in four months.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Still, the conversation was focused on “The Mosquito Bowl” and on Okinawa, where Berg, whose father served as a Marine, as did Bissinger’s, went to research the script. Marine historians walked him across the battlefields where Tony Butkovich, Dave Schreiner, Bob Bauman and George Murphy were killed and down to the Cornerstone of Peace, the memorial that bears the names of more than 240,000 people who died in the battle.

Below, Berg talks about how “Chicago Hope” and a lunchtime question to James Mangold turned him into a director, why Ray Nicholson deserves respect for owning his last name, what a “Friday Night Lights” reboot needs before anyone writes a script and the “Shocker” drive-in prank he calls the greatest actor moment of his career.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

You're one of the rare actors-turned-directors who seems to genuinely love being behind the camera. When did you get the bug?

When I was in college, I was acting and my school didn’t have a film department. I went to this little school called Macalester College in St. Paul, Minnesota. There was another tiny little school called St. Thomas, and they did. So I would go down there and take little film classes and make little 16-millimeter, sometimes Super 8 films. I always just liked the whole world of it. I liked acting. I liked theater. I liked building sets. I liked playing around with cameras.

I moved to L.A. thinking I was going to go to film school, and a series of twists and turns led me to doing a play in like 1990 at the Odyssey Theatre and that started me as an actor. I had a nice little acting career going, and then I got on this show “Chicago Hope.” Each episode was nine days and like 14 hours of shooting. I sat there and started hating acting on a television show. It just became like a treadmill to oblivion in my mind.

But I had this front-row seat to all these different directors, and most of those directors were kind of like failed feature directors back then. These were guys that all thought they were going to be Scorsese, and it didn’t work out for whatever reason. They would come in with all this passion to direct an episode of “Chicago Hope,” and for two days, I’d feel their passion and then the reality of TV scheduling would just turn them into factory workers. But I got to learn from being there and seeing that. It was kind of like my film school.

There was a guy named Bill D’Elia, who was the executive producer of “Chicago Hope,” who let me direct my first episode. David Kelley let me write my first episode, and then he let us produce the episode that I wrote. That was a real game changer for me. And there was another director named Oz Scott, who kind of took me under his wing and let me in on his process.

Then the final moment that really pushed me over the edge: I was acting in a movie called “Cop Land,” and I had a small part. De Niro was in it, Harvey Keitel, Ray Liotta. This was before Harvey Weinstein had been revealed to be what Harvey Weinstein is. He was the biggest superstar producer in town. And there was this young filmmaker in the middle of it all. He had written the script, and he was arguing with Weinstein and with De Niro and I was just sitting there waiting for my one line. I finally walked up to him at lunch. I barely knew him. I’m like, “Excuse me, how do I get your job?” And it was James Mangold. He goes, “You got to write. Do you have an idea?” I said I did. He said, “Write it.”

So every night after we’d wrap “Cop Land,” I would go back to my hotel instead of going out and partying with all the other actors and I would just write, write, write. Mangold, and I’ve told him this, was the final catalyst that made me jump because I saw what he was doing and I wanted that. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Mangold finally earned his first directing nomination for “A Complete Unknown.” You two come from the same school of filmmaking, it seems.

Certainly not an overnight success. This has been earned for a long, long time. James Mangold has definitely earned it.

War movies can be a tough sell. People hear “true story,” watch some men die and move on with their lives. “The Mosquito Bowl” made me think about how we send babies to war. Was that part of the inspiration?

No. My dad was a Marine. He served in Korea. Buzz Bissinger, who wrote the book, his father was a Marine. Buzz and I are cousins. Our dads were good friends. We both grew up sort of understanding the Marine Corps, understanding what it means when you ask Marines to go. Because when you ask them to go, they will go.

When I was writing the script, I spent a lot of time at Parris Island with these 17-, 18-year-old recruits, real recruits today and I started writing the script at a little motel right off the base. Their youth was something that was really seared into me, as it was from the book.

But after Parris Island, what really fired me up to make this film the way I did was I went to Okinawa, where the final battle of the movie takes place, where these young men, Butkovich and Schreiner and Bauman and Murphy, all died. The Marine historians took me on a tour of the island. I started in the center of the island, where the invasion started and I went over Hacksaw Ridge and into the caves. There are still marks on the walls from where the Japanese soldiers pulled the pins on their grenades and blew themselves up because they didn’t want to surrender. You can see where those suicides took place. Then I went all the way to the southern tip of the island, where it ended and there are these cliffs where Okinawan women were throwing themselves off, holding their babies. And then there’s the peace memorial, with the names of the people who died on that island. The power of that experience was really quite awesome inside of me, and that got me going.

And the kicker was, after they toured me, the Marines said, “Would you like to see our current military bases on Okinawa?” I said, “Sure.” And I didn’t realize that we have Marines and current military on these massive bases right now, today. While we’re having this conversation, they’re there. We have aircraft carriers, troop movers, attack aircraft, attack helicopters, missile systems. There is a massive military operation going on right now.

I met with the commanding general of the base, and we’re in his office and there’s a big window behind him and there are F-35s flying constantly behind him. I said, “Sir, can I ask you a question?” He said, “Yes.” I said, “What the fuck is going on here?” Literally how I asked the question. I had no idea, and I’d wager that most people who read you don’t know this is happening. He says, “I’ll tell you, that’s a good question.” He gets up, and he has a giant map of the South China Sea. He goes, “It’s all about this” and he points to this tiny little island, Taiwan. He goes, “They want it” and he points above it on the map, China. “It’s my job to make sure they know they can’t have it.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid4' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

And I’m thinking, OK, a war movie. Do we need another war movie? Have we learned our lesson? Seventy-five million people were killed globally in World War II. All it takes right now is for a Chinese aircraft and an American aircraft to play games with each other and clip wings, and we could be in a really bad spot.

So for me, seeing the young Marines today on the island of Okinawa, ready to go do exactly what the Marines did in the 1940s, ready to go fight, made me think, they’re young. War is fucking hell. And it’s possible to hold the two truths. You can respect the military. You can understand the need for a military and make sure we protect and honor those men and women who are willing to go. That’s truth one. And truth two is we need to do everything we fucking can to not go to war. We need diplomats. We need peacemakers. We need to understand what happens when you send young men into war.

That's why I made the film the way I did. I didn't turn it into a character study of those guys. I wanted to immerse the audience in what it looks like when young men get their faces blown off. Some critics have responded very well to that, and others haven't and that's fine by me.

There's such a disconnect now. So much of modern war is fought from a distance, almost like a video game. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid5' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

For sure. We’re being told that drones and AI weapon systems are great because they’re saving lives. But think about it this way: In 1943, when we would go fight on these islands in the Pacific, you had 5,000, 10,000 Japanese on an island. You had 10,000 Marines ready to go breach that island and have this fight. They didn’t have drones back then, but they had massive naval artillery bombardments, which you can think of as drones. Because the theory is, we won’t send men into an active war zone. We’ll use bombs and stay back and blow up the island and kill all the Japanese, and then the Marines can go in. That’ll reduce the human risk. But it didn’t work, because the Japanese just hid in the caves and then the Americans had to go and they had to fight to the death.

Well, the same thing’s happening in Ukraine now. The drones are keeping people back, but unfortunately, eventually, human beings must engage with each other, face to face or bullet to bullet. So these were the big ideas lurking underneath. Yeah, we’re making a World War II film. Yes, it’s a story of football players and these were beautiful men who died. But I was asking people to question war.

Man is violent. There’s always been war. But when you see what happened when Outlook crashed [on Nov. 12], this planet cannot absorb a world war. We can barely absorb what’s going on in the Middle East right now. We can absorb what’s going on in eastern Ukraine. But if we go at it with China, it’s game over.

People say we're one person away from having a bad day and then ending everything as we know it.

There's a quote I was thinking about when I made this film. Have you ever heard of Stewart Brand? He's a big thinker, kind of like Oppenheimer-level. He had a simple quote. He said, “We are as gods and might as well get good at it.” And that's never felt more true. We now have the power to utterly destroy this planet like that. Do we want to do that? I'm going to go out on a limb: No, we don't. Look at where we are with the weapon systems, with the technology, with the hostility, with the greed. We are as gods. How do we want to behave?

I just got back three weeks ago from a funeral for a friend of mine who committed suicide as soon as he got out of the military. And I’ve been to several funerals. It’s a rough business, war. If there’s a scale between peace and war, I don’t think any one movie is going to tilt anything. I understand why deterrence is important and why we need to be strong and why we need a military, and I love these men and women and I am pretty unapologetic about that. I feel it for the young men and women at Parris Island right now who, for multiple reasons, are willing to serve in the United States Marine Corps. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid6' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

When I screened the film at Camp Pendleton for 900 Marines, I told them I love them and I respect their job and I sincerely hope they move through their entire careers as Marines and they get great values and they learn grit and resilience and they make friendships. I hope they do all of that, and they never have to kill a person. They never have to fight. And they just looked at me and nodded.

I showed this movie to Admiral McRaven and General Petraeus, and afterward Admiral McRaven gave me a hug and he was emotional. He said, “This is what people should be seeing. This is what war does to people.” And he said something interesting. This is Admiral McRaven, a legendary American military leader. He said, “Peter, there is no greater pacifist on this planet than me.” And General Petraeus was nodding his head. These are guys who have to go to the funerals for people who’ve died. They have to go to the funerals for military personnel who’ve committed suicide on the way out because they couldn’t deal with it. They understand the cost. They understand the need for deterrence.

Bill Maher tried to tell me that I didn’t understand the need for deterrence. I’m like, yes, I do. I do. You can hold both truths. We have to have a strong hammer, but we have to also try and figure out other ways to function without using that hammer. Because once you use that hammer, what happens in our movie happens. Seventy-five million people died.

My brother served in the Army, and my nephew is serving now. I'm a fierce advocate for the military, but I feel like we treat our vets like shit.

Of course we do. We spend millions and billions of dollars making the soldiers, making the equipment and the second they’re done, take a number and go to the VA hospital. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid7' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

I know a lot of vets. Ray Mendoza is a very good friend of mine. He directed “Warfare.” He came out of the Navy SEALs, and he worked on a lot of my movie sets and I watched him just create a career in this business and manage his stressors from being a Navy SEAL for 20-odd years. It’s not like all veterans need help. Marcus Luttrell, his brother Morgan Luttrell, who became a congressman. There's a lot of veterans who can get themselves going, but there are a lot who can’t.

These were all reasons. People are like, “Why would you want to make another World War II film? ‘Saving Private Ryan’ was a pretty good film.” Yes, it was. Oh, yes, it was. But this is a different time.

“Deepwater Horizon” and “Patriots Day” are my two favorites of yours, and I'd argue this is your strongest ensemble yet. Are you directing actors better than ever, or did you just have a group doing something you'd never seen?

Maybe a little of both. I do feel like I’m getting more comfortable. I feel fortunate that I’ve been able to have a long career and succeed and fail and learn how to collaborate and find people I trust, and that made me better. So I’m more excited and comfortable just being a filmmaker. I really love it.

With the actors, I really credit the book and Buzz Bissinger, because when a script is born from the truth and you reference two films, “Deepwater” and “Patriots Day,” those were true stories. I was able to go into those worlds and meet the people and find the truth. I love nonfiction because I can find the truth. And once I find the truth, I can hopefully get it on the page and I can bring it to the set and I can talk to the actors and the actors can meet the real people and experience the truth and that helps make their performances more truthful. All of them were just really talented actors who responded to the truth of the story, and that made them lock in a little bit harder.

Ray Nicholson is particularly interesting to me, and I love him very much. I've had long talks with him. The whole nepo baby thing. Can you imagine trying to be an actor and your father is Jack Nicholson? Good fucking luck, bro. And you kind of look like your father.

Jack Nicholson is my favorite [actor]. “Cuckoo's Nest” is my personal favorite film. And what I've said to Ray is, what's so fascinating about where you are now and where you can go is that you have a chance to find your own way and be your own guy. There's a lot of people who have not seen “One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest” or “Chinatown.” You have your own unique energy. You'll have that last name, but you are not your father and that gives you the opportunity to do something completely unique. And you do have your father's genes in you, which is a good thing, because everyone who has not experienced the Jack Nicholson gene gets to get a taste of it, but in a different way. Hold your head up high.

The fact that he’s able to stand on his own two feet as his son is, I think, beautiful. I’m really impressed with how he’s able to own the reality of, yes, I am Jack Nicholson’s son and I am going to have my own career. That’s respect. I tip my hat to that young man. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid8' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

This one is for me and my sister. “Shocker” is the movie that made us “friends” in the sibling sense because we watched it over 100 times. Are there movies that changed your life in ways their makers might never know?

One that comes to mind is “Billy Jack.” The quote from the movie is, “When I see her humiliated and embarrassed and hurt, well, sir, I just go berserk.” That was the first time I remember, as a little kid, just trembling in a movie theater and I quote that still to this day, all the time.

But I’ll tell you one funny “Shocker” story that I think you might appreciate. There are two things I took from that film. Wes Craven was just an incredibly sweet human being, and it blew my mind that this lovely, sweet, gentle man could have this imagination. That was kind of my first lesson: Don’t judge a book by the cover. I think he was a teacher for a while. Just the most gentle, lovely man and then he would come up with these wild, terrifying stories.

I was making a film in Mississippi, and I went out with the cast to a drive-in and we all went to see “Shocker.” I think Ally Sheedy was in the car, and Phoebe Cates and Kyle Secor, just a bunch of actors. And there's hundreds of cars. It was an old-school drive-in theater, speaker in the window. And the car next to us had these four teenagers, Southern boys and they're smoking weed, just clouds of weed and they're mesmerized by the movie. They're watching me fight Mitch, and they're just so stoned and so locked in. I got out of the car, and I sneaked around to their window and I just knocked on it and it's me. They turned and they looked at me, and they looked at the movie and they looked at me and they freaked out. Just screaming. It was the greatest actor moment of my career. Can you imagine? You’re a 17-year-old in Mississippi, stoned out of your mind, staring at this movie outside at a drive-in and the actor from the movie is in your face.

The “Friday Night Lights” reboot is in development at Peacock, and you've called it a complete reinvention. What does Dillon look like in 2026 or 2027?

If it's a complete reinvention, it probably won't be Dillon. If you're going to do a reboot of “Friday Night Lights,” you have to look at what made “Friday Night Lights” work. If you trace that back to its genesis, it's Buzz Bissinger again. In the mid-'80s, he moved his family to Odessa, Texas, lived with the Permian Panthers football team and moved into the community of Odessa for over a year. He's an investigative journalist, and he went very deep. If you read the book, it's about much, much more than football. It's about community and family and educational systems and racism and love and hatred and winning. There's some deep themes in that book. That led to the movie, which then led to the TV show, but without the book and without the soul of Bissinger in there, it wouldn't have worked.

So for us to do a remake, what first has to happen and he knows this, is Buzz has to go into another community in 2026, 2027. It could be Texas, it could be Ohio, it could be Florida, anywhere football is played. It’s a different world right now. We didn’t have these cell phones. So we need to have the origin story done right, and that means before a script is written, there has to be something else written, whether that’s a book or a detailed, long-form piece of journalism. I don’t want to just do it to do it. But what does excite me is if somebody approaches it as a piece of cultural anthropology or a sociological exploration of a community in today’s Americana. Then I think you have the chance of success. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid9' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Do you ever think about acting again?

Not really. Little parts. What do you got for me?

Someone online suggested you'd make a great Buddy Ryan, the architect of the 1985 Bears defense. Call Michael Mann.

That's amazing. Michael's my mentor. He produced “The Kingdom”; he produced “Hancock.” He saw an early show I did called “Wonderland,” about a psychiatric hospital in New York that was killed instantly by ABC and he responded so well to that. He's one of my favorite people on planet Earth. He's a great human being.

articles.title: FCC Bid Challenging ABC's TV Licenses Halted in Major Win for Network
articles.summary: The ruling is a major setback for the administration in the government's campaign against ABC and national media.
articles.content:
ABC has won a court order barring the Federal Communications Commission from taking further action against the network amid the government's efforts to possibly strip the company of its local broadcast licenses.

U.S. District Judge Loren Alikhan on Wednesday rebuffed the FCC 's bid to dismiss the lawsuit, finding that the agency likely violated ABC's First Amendment rights by weaponizing its regulatory authority to retaliate against the network for protected speech and pressure it to change its editorial decisions.

The Disney-owned company sued the FCC earlier this year after the Brendan Carr-led agency called for an early review of ABC's broadcast licenses. The renewal prompted concerns of retaliation since it followed an investigation into Disney's diversity practices and ABC late-night host Kimmy Kimmel angering President Donald Trump with a joke. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories TV TV Ratings: 'Dancing With the Stars' Records Another Huge Finale TV 'Dancing With the Stars' Names Historic Season 35 Winner: See All the Scores, Who Won

In Wednesday's ruling, the court said that Carr's conduct is "powerful evidence" of the FCC's "retaliatory motive."

"It is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel’s skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings," Alikhan wrote. She pointed to Carr's comment that "we can do this the easy way or the hard way" and that "these companies can find ways to take action on Kimmel, or there is going to be additional work for the FCC ahead."

The FCC has maintained that the early license renewal proceedings are merely "in aid" of its investigation into Disney's employment practices and would've occurred regardless.

The court was unconvinced, finding that it "does not find that explanation to be credible." It stressed that Trump has targeted ABC for several years. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The FCC has also launched a separate inquiry into The View , which it argued is not a “bona fide” news program and therefore is not exempt from FCC equal opportunity rules. This came after an appearance by James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for the Texas Senate, in February. ABC said in an earlier filing that the FCC “now appears poised to find that The View must provide equal opportunities to all legally qualified political candidates if it interviews one candidate on the show, which would represent a reversal of decades of agency precedent.”

articles.title: GTA 6 Every Major Missable Mission & Reward in Each Chapter of the Game
articles.summary: Courtesy of Rockstar Games GTA 6 is packed with optional missions, unique weapons, hidden rewards, and collectibles that are easy to overlook while progressing through its story. Unfortunately, some of that content becomes permanently unavailable once certain missions are completed, meaning you can lose access to rewards and side stories without realizing it. Several of these opportunities are tied […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google GTA 6 is packed with optional missions, unique weapons, hidden rewards, and collectibles that are easy to overlook while progressing through its story. Unfortunately, some of that content becomes permanently unavailable once certain missions are completed, meaning you can lose access to rewards and side stories without realizing it.

Several of these opportunities are tied to specific story missions or chapter transitions, while others require you to respond to a phone call or complete an activity before its timer expires. GTA 6 also doesn't offer a traditional mission replay menu, making it especially important to know when to stop and explore before advancing the story.

Note: This guide is being actively updated as more of GTA 6's missable missions, rewards, and optional content are discovered. If something isn't listed yet, we'll add it as soon as we've verified the details.

Chapter 1 has the largest concentration of missable content in GTA 6 . Jason's Key Lento home eventually becomes inaccessible, taking several collectibles and optional activities with it. There are also opportunities that disappear much earlier than the chapter's conclusion, so don't wait until the final mission to start checking things off.

During "Don Gone," Jason gets involved in a situation with Donnie and his associates. Before getting rid of Donnie's car, make sure to open its trunk and collect the H&L .38 Revolver. This is a unique weapon, and the opportunity to obtain it disappears once the vehicle is gone.

While you're inside Donnie's trailer during the same mission, check the bathroom for his aviator sunglasses. These are another easy pickup to overlook while progressing through the objective. Make sure you collect both items before leaving the area.

Jason's neighbor Shirley has two optional favors available during Chapter 1: "Get Shirley's Rum" and "Steal the Scooter." These are short side activities, but they're exclusive to this part of the story and disappear once the chapter's transition begins.

Complete both while Shirley's requests are still available. They're easy to overlook if you're focused on the main missions, and there's no later opportunity to return to her original requests.

After completing "Day Release," Jason may receive a call from Lucia asking him to pick her up from work. This begins the optional mission "Clock Out," which requires Jason to reach the Key Lento Community Center before 4 p.m.

The call doesn't appear in every playthrough, so keep an eye out for it. If you receive it, prioritize the pickup rather than letting the in-game day pass. Missing the deadline means losing the opportunity to complete the activity.

After completing "Feng Shui," Jason can purchase a custom gold necklace for Lucia at The Siren's Chest jewelry store in southern Key Lento. The optional errand, "Buy Lucia a Necklace," costs $475 and gives Jason a relationship boost with Lucia. The chain is engraved with Tommy's name, making it a meaningful gift that also becomes useful later in the story.

Don't skip this purchase if you want the necklace. It's exclusive to Chapter 1, and Lucia can use it as collateral during Chapter 2 when Linda demands payment for the Starlet Motel room. Paying the outstanding balance during "Behind on Payments" allows Lucia to recover it

The end of Chapter 1 comes with a financial reset that can catch you off guard. Before completing "Recalibration," transfer the money you want to preserve into Family Savings through the BuckMe app.Cash outside Family Savings can be lost during the transition, so don't leave money sitting in Jason's wallet or other accounts. Depositing around $5,000 is a useful target if you want to start the next chapter with some financial breathing room.

It's also worth making a separate manual save before accepting Mattia's offer and starting "Tourist Trap." That mission begins the sequence that takes Jason and Lucia away from Key Lento, removing access to the house and its remaining pickups.

After completing "Buck Me" and receiving the relevant phone call, Jason can undertake the optional mission "Find the Lost Drugs." Four search areas appear across the swamps of Mariana County, where Jason must recover packages of cocaine. Once you've collected the drugs, take them to a fence to sell them.

This mission is exclusive to Chapter 1, so don't leave it until after the chapter transition. There's another reason to complete it early: Donnie offers a better payout than Brian, but his drop-off location becomes unavailable after "Clear Skies." Selling the haul to Donnie earns $3,400, compared to Brian's $2,720.

Chapter 2 shifts the focus to Port Gellhorn, where the Starlet Motel serves as an important home base. The motel eventually stops being the characters' safehouse, taking some of its collectibles and optional encounters with it.

Make one final trip through the building before using the room interaction that begins the move to Vice City. The motel's public areas and the departure sequence are easy to confuse, so don't assume you'll be able to return to everything once you leave.

One of the rewards tied to Chapter 2 actually begins much earlier. After completing "Feng Shui" in Chapter 1, Jason can purchase a necklace for Lucia at The Siren's Chest for $475.

If you do, the necklace can end up in Linda's possession at the Starlet Motel. During the motel's payment-related encounters, settle the outstanding charges to recover it. Check the amount Linda requests and make sure you have enough cash available; the recovery is tied to paying the motel bill, not simply picking the necklace up from a room.

Don't overlook this if you purchased the necklace earlier and want to get it back.

While visiting the Starlet Motel, look for Wyman in the parking lot. He's working on his Dominator and can use a little help getting the engine started.

When the encounter is available, speak with him as Lucia and follow the prompts while he works. This is an optional interaction tied to the motel's Chapter 2 period, so take the opportunity to complete it before moving out.

Chapter 3 introduces several particularly valuable missables, including unique weapons, a vehicle, and optional mission rewards. Some of these opportunities are tied to specific story missions, while others depend on responding to optional activities before their timers expire.

The chapter's conclusion also removes access to Boobie's Bayside apartment, making it important to collect its publications and claim Vanessa's vehicle before completing "The Cartel Heist."

One of Chapter 3's more involved rewards is Vanessa's pink Pfister Growler. To unlock it, you need to investigate the clues found around the Bayside apartment and use them to access Vanessa's laptop.

The three clues are "Muffins," a queen, and the number 15. Once you've entered the correct information, open Vanessa's messages and look for the conversation that reveals a garage code: 92665 .

Head to the Del Rio Boulevard Garage in La Perle, near Auntie's Place, and enter the code. Inside, you'll find Vanessa's pink Growler. Drive it out to register the vehicle and claim it for yourself.

Make sure to do this before completing "The Cartel Heist." The garage and its vehicle become inaccessible after Chapter 3, making this one of the more involved rewards you can permanently miss.

During "The Missing Link," Lucia gets caught up in a shootout after photographing the cartel. Once the fighting begins, make sure to return to the photo room where Monty was previously encountered.

Monty's 1992 Pistol is lying on the floor. Pick it up before continuing through the mission, as leaving the room without collecting it means losing the opportunity to obtain this unique weapon.

The mission "Safe Word" offers another worthwhile reward for those willing to explore its optional objectives. During the safecracking practice at Raul's compound, Lucia gets an opportunity to open a safe.

Don't end the practice session early. Complete all three stages of the process: drilling through the safe, guiding the cable through its mechanism, and holding the door open to finish cracking it.

Once the safe is open, collect Gil's Kalinga .50 and the additional $1,500 inside. Leaving the practice session before opening the safe means missing both rewards.

After completing "Join a Street Race" and "Bumper to Bumper," Jason can receive an invitation to take part in "Race Against Yago." Keep an eye out for the hourglass marker, as this optional activity is time-sensitive.

Complete the race as soon as it appears. Winning rewards you with approximately $3,800 and unlocks the follow-up "Brother to Brother" mission. Missing the race can also prevent you from completing Yago's optional questline, making this one of the more important timed activities to watch for.

The optional mission chain "Dubious Provenance" is another Chapter 3 activity worth paying attention to. During its first part, you encounter Halifax and must decide how to handle his offer.

If you decline Halifax's initial offer, you'll have an opportunity to contact him later. Make that call before Chapter 3 ends to unlock the remaining parts of the mission chain. Letting the opportunity expire means losing access to the follow-up missions and their rewards.

Completing the later parts can provide additional cash and jewelry, as well as the opportunity to obtain the Vapid '32 Hustler. Don't leave Halifax's story unfinished when the chapter's final mission approaches.

During "Bricked Up," you can find a red bag containing Boobie's Bricks in the first room. Make sure to collect it before leaving the area.

The bag contains $3,500 and contributes to the mission's Professional bonus. It's a small detail that's easy to overlook during the mission, especially if you're focused on completing the main objective.

Chapter 4 moves Jason and Lucia into the Y Hotel as they prepare for the airport heist. There are two optional missions that can disappear before the chapter ends, along with a unique weapon that you can easily walk past during the heist itself.

The airport heist isn't the chapter's final point of no return. You still have time to explore Vice City afterward, so use that window to finish anything left open. The bigger deadline comes when the message at the Y Hotel front desk triggers "Sunset."

After completing "Party Hard," Andrea may contact Jason or Lucia about Felipe, who can be found at a bar in Millport. This begins the optional mission "Bad Driver!"

You have a choice when dealing with Felipe. Killing him provides an immediate $20,000 reward, while sparing him allows him to offer his car later through the follow-up mission "Collect Felipe's Gift."

Either outcome has its own reward, so consider making a manual save before confronting him if you want to experience both possibilities. Most importantly, complete "Bad Driver!" before starting "Power Play." Once that mission begins, the opportunity disappears.

Lucia can receive a phone call from Shayna that begins the optional mission "This Is a Free Call From…" Shayna needs a ride after being released from prison, and the activity is exclusive to Lucia.

Once the hourglass marker appears, head to the pickup location as soon as possible. This is a time-sensitive mission, and waiting too long can cause the opportunity to expire permanently.

During the final ground shootout in "VCIA Takedown," Jason has an opportunity to collect Francisco's LMG-6.

When the game switches back to Jason and he is defending Andrea while she loads the bags, look for the weapon on the ground. Pick it up before entering the getaway van. Those who rush straight toward the vehicle can easily leave this unique weapon behind.

During "Passing the Torch," you can find Pilot Pete's KZ-59 in the back room of the hangar at Sundown Private Airfield.

Importantly, the KZ-59 is a unique rifle, not a vehicle. Take the time to search the hangar before leaving the mission area, as the weapon is tied to this opportunity.

At the time of writing, there are no confirmed permanently missable optional mission chains, weapons, or collectibles exclusive to Chapter 5. You can return to free roam after completing the story, so there's less pressure to clear the map before reaching the finale.

However, Chapter 5 contains important decisions that affect the ending. Before confirming "Protective Custody" at Abe's office, consider making a separate manual save. The mission leads directly into the final sequence, and the game does not offer a traditional mission replay menu.

Players pursuing a particular ending should also pay attention to their relationship level, both characters' Criminal Profiles , and the money held in Family Savings . One ending route requires $2 million in Family Savings before proceeding, alongside other conditions and decisions during the finale. If you want to explore different outcomes, preserve a save before committing to the mission rather than relying on the post-credits return to free roam.

articles.title: This Vintage Boba Fett Figure Has One Extra Detail That Makes It Even More Valuable to Collectors
articles.summary: While almost any of Kenner's vintage Star Wars toys are worth getting your hands on, there are some that are more valuable than others. Of course, the original line is something everyone would love to own, especially the figures with the double telescoping lightsabers. However, we all know that the Holy Grail of Kenner's Star […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google While almost any of Kenner's vintage Star Wars toys are worth getting your hands on, there are some that are more valuable than others. Of course, the original line is something everyone would love to own, especially the figures with the double telescoping lightsabers . However, we all know that the Holy Grail of Kenner's Star Wars toys is the missile firing Boba Fett that could fetch you over a million dollars . In fact, that figure became so coveted that it made all other Boba Fett figures more valuable. However, one fan boosted the value of his figure by getting it autographed by the bounty hunter himself, along with a pretty cool message.

As showcased by the fan on Reddit their Boba Fett figure belongs to The Power of the Force series, which came much later than Kenner's original and highly coveted line. It features the red and orange cardback, signifying that it's pretty common even among its own line. However, the standout feature is actor Jeremy Bulloch's autograph in silver ink, with the message "Stay Cool", along with the date. Depending on which format Bullock followed, it was either autographed a day before Star Wars Day, May 3rd; or on March 5th, 2000. Given the fact that Bulloch was English, it's likely the latter.

If you look at the hierarchy of popularity in Kenner's Star Wars line, those from The Power of the Force series will rank pretty low. Even today, the figures aren't worth much more than their original retail prices, and are pretty easy to come by if you know where to look. However, there are two kinds of collectors: those who do it for the monetary value of an item, and those that do it for the love. If you belong to the latter, you probably wouldn't be too fussed about grading, condition, variants, and all the other stuff hardcore collectors look at. You'll be happy with your sealed vintage Boba Fett, no matter which series it's from or if it has a tiny scratch. The fact that it just happens to have actor Jeremy Bulloch's autograph on it is a bonus. The collector has wrapped it in a plastic bag to preserve the toy and the autograph, but I'd suggest getting something more robust if they want it to last.

Even if it's by the original actor themselves, autographs don't boost the value of vintage action figures by too much. Seasoned collectors will still prefer the other criteria, like rarity, condition, and popularity, over autographs. However, if you're someone who collects these things for the love of the franchise, an autograph by the original actor is like a dream come true. Especially if you got the autograph from them yourself. While a missile-shooting, pristine condition Boba Fett figure from a very specific year is the epitome of vintage Star Wars toys, many of us would be happy with the common figure signed by the original actor himself.

Do you have any signed action figures or collectibles? Let us know in the comments below.

articles.title: Judge Sides With ABC In First Amendment Lawsuit Against FCC; Puts Halt To Agency's Early License Renewal Proceeding
articles.summary: A federal judge has largely sided with ABC in its First Amendment lawsuit claiming that an FCC order to review its broadcast licenses was a retaliatory act by the Trump administration designed to chill its content, whether that be news coverage or jokes from Jimmy Kimmel. U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan issued a preliminary injunction […]
articles.content:
A federal judge has halted the FCC 's early license renewal order for ABC 's stations, granting the network a preliminary injunction that it said was retaliatory in violation of the First Amendment .

The network is the first major media conglomerate to challenge the FCC's wave of investigations since the start of Donald Trump 's second term.

ABC filed suit against the FCC in August, claiming that the agency was violating the First Amendment as it ordered the network's broadcast stations to submit their licenses to an early review. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani struck a personal note during a press briefing Wednesday about the postponement of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade due to a major storm.

"Many New Yorkers, myself included, as well as millions around the world were looking forward to the parade being held tomorrow," the mayor said. "I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences. Yet safety has to come first. On Saturday, when balloons climb into the sky, every New Yorker, and everyone visiting, will be able to take in a show that is both truly spectacular and also safe." Organizers and city officials, made the call earlier Wednesday to push the 100th annual edition of the parade to Saturday morning, when the forecast calls for sunny skies and temperatures in the 40s. A Nor'easter, a classic storm pattern, is expected to bring drenching rain and high winds to New York and many other parts of the Northeast on Thursday and into Friday. Mamdani, hobbled by a recent Achilles tear, said he will miss Saturday's parade due to pending surgery and "doctor's orders." But while he walked with a limp, the mayor showed he hadn't lost a step mentally. When a reporter asked about the blowing up of the signature balloons, an annual public ritual held on Thanksgiving Eve near the parade route, Mamdani quipped, “It's the only kind of inflation we support in New York City .”

Will Coss, an executive producer and VP at Macy's who oversees the retailer's events, said there will not be a second chance to watch the night-before inflation of the balloons due to the complex logistics of the postponement. He was also asked about the lineup for the event, which could change given that some marching bands (like the one from the University of Albama) are planning to leave town to play at college football games or other events. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The parade is set to include a number of other special guests and celebrities appearing on floats or performing. An “All-Star Broadway Thanksgiving Day Celebration” will feature performers from new and long-running Broadway productions in a special 10-minute medley .

Coss said it is "an evolving conversation" about potential replacements or planned participants possibly bowing out due to conflicts or travel plans. "We've been in communication with all of our participants, from our bands, to our performance groups, to our performing talent. We are optimistic that we're going to be able to maintain the parade that we set out to produce, and to deliver to New York City."

The parade remains a major TV draw, with last year’s pulling in 34.3 million viewers across NBC and Peacock, its biggest combined audience on record. By slotting it in on Saturday morning from 8:30 a.m. to noon ET, NBC should be able to have access to a good-sized audience before college football takes over. Still, the viewership patterns on a more conventional Saturday morning versus those on a weekday holiday with preparations for the Thanksgiving feast providing a supply of captive viewers, will be interesting to watch.

In place of the live event, NBC and Peacock will re-air the 2025 edition of the parade on Thursday morning. Mindful of the unusual dynamic in play this year, the network and streamer will double-run the same ads on both Thursday and Saturday to ensure the scale and impact nets out to a satisfying level for buyers.

It is the first time since it began in 1924 that the parade has ever been postponed. In 1971, balloons were grounded by inclement weather but the parade was still held. World War II forced the cancellation of the parade from 1942 to 1944, and the Covid pandemic in 2020 led to organizers converting it into a television-only event around the Herald Square location of Macy’s Department Store.

This year’s parade is especially significant to Macy’s and NBC, with the latter celebrating its centennial in broadcasting. To help mark the milestone, the parade is set to have 100 of its trademark large balloons.

The importance of NBC's 100th anniversary is likely to have played a role in the rescheduling. Parent company NBCUniversal, announced early this week that this year's parade set a revenue record. A windswept and soggy edition of the annual TV fixture would surely have presented myriad production challenges. It possibly would also have left advertisers tuning in to see compromised signage and balloons (some of them branded) swirling precariously around the streets.

"We want to ensure that we're delivering a parade that's not only incredible and spectacular, but one also that doesn't come at the expense of anyone's safety," Mamdani said.

Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Is Avatar 4 really happening? The internet is hyped about word that Disney has greenlit the fourth installment in James Cameron's milestone sci-fi franchise. This latest buzz comes from reports on Disney's Upfronts of its upcoming slate of projects, which was previewed during a presentation in Argentina. With Avatar 4 already occupying a release slot, and Disney now highlighting the film at the Upfronts, some fans have all the evidence they need to jump to the conclusion that production on the film is ready to go.

But is that really the case? There was a lot that seemed to shift after the release of Avatar: Fire and Ash , and the franchise's future has felt far more uncertain. As it stands, there isn't going to be more Avatar for quite a while, even though some of the fourth film is already shot.

Avatar was always planned to be at least a five-film franchise, with Cameron having hired additional stars like Michelle Yeoh ( Blade Runner 2099 ) to join the franchise. Additionally, Cameron used the time during and after shooting Avatar: Fire and Ash to shoot additional scenes for Avatar 4 – specifically the younger cast members like Britain Dalton (Lo'ak), Trinity Jo-Li Bliss (Tuk), and Jack Champion (Spider), who took another step toward becoming the new protagonists of the franchise in the third film. Avatar 4 is said to include a time jump , which will account for how the younger characters inevitably grow and age in the years between Fire and Ash and the fourth film. So Cameron made sure to get any introductory and/or flashback footage in the can while he had the chance.

Thanks to that foresight, Cameron and the cast of the Avatar series have had a well-earned break – at least this year. Earlier this year, Avatar producer Rae Sanchini made it clear that the machine was gearing up again, and that Avatar 4 would be going into production soon .

“Right now we’re figuring out the schedule,” Sanchini told Inverse . “We’re working hard on it right now, budgeting, scheduling, planning, building out our new pipeline for them. As far as we’re concerned, we’re full speed ahead.”

In that same report, however, Sanchini also noted that Avatar 4 's current release date of December 21, 2029, is now "tentative." He described the need for restructuring the production plans and scaling up to meet the demands of the next chapters. Behind the scenes, that mandate for "restructuring" is also said to be Disney putting pressure on the creative team to bring down the massive costs of the films . Each Avatar sequel has seen its budget soar to somewhere between $300-$400 million; even though they both cleared the billion-dollar mark at the box office, Fire and Ash topped out at just under $1.5 billion – a steep drop-off from the second film, The Way of Water, which earned over $2.3 billion.

More importantly, there have been signs of Avatar fatigue, both culturally and creatively. The new generation of viewers hasn't made the films and their lore the kind of cultural staple that the franchise once was. Meanwhile, James Cameron has made no secret that as he's aging, making more Avatar sequels feels less and less like a priority for him, personally.

"There’s been momentum in the Avatar universe for 21 years at this point because we started in 2005,” Cameron said while receiving the 2026 Governor General’s Performing Arts Award. “It’s been kind of an unbroken continuum. So this is the point where I’m looking at the landscape and asking, ‘What are the other stories I want to tell? How many of them do I need to direct myself versus writing and/or producing with other filmmakers?’”

It seems that the big unanswered question that is hanging over the Avatar franchise is not whether it will continue, but whether it will continue with James Cameron at the helm. And if the motion we're seeing is any indication, Disney will be answering that question sometime next year.

Avatar 4 is currently scheduled for December 21, 2029.
